exampleAnswers.title: Verifying Continuity at a Point Using the Definition

question.text:
Consider the following function: \[ g(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{x}{2}+1 , & x \neq -1 \\ 0 , & x=-1 \end{cases} \] Which of the following statements are true regarding $g(x)?$

  1. $g(x)$ is defined at $x=-1$
  2. $\lim\limits_{x\to \,\left(-1\right)} g(x)$ exists
  3. $\lim\limits_{x\to \,\left(-1\right)} g(x)=g(-1)$
  4. $g(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=-1$
question.explanation:
To test for continuity of $f(x)$ at a point $x=c$, we need to check three conditions:

  1. Does $f(c)$ exist?

  2. Does $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)$ exist?

  3. Does $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x) = f(c)?$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Using the expression for the second branch of the function, we obtain that \[ g(-1)= 0. \] So, $g(x)$ is defined at $x=-1.$ $\:\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Statement II is true. By calculating the one-sided limits, we get the following: \begin{align} \lim\limits_{x\to \left(-1\right)^-} g(x) &=\lim\limits_{x\to \left(-1\right)^-}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}+1\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(-1)}{2}+1\\[5pt] &=\dfrac 12 \\[10pt] \lim\limits_{x\to \left(-1\right)^+} g(x) &=\lim\limits_{x\to \left(-1\right)^+} \left(\dfrac{x}{2}+1\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{(-1)}{2}+1\\[5pt] &=\dfrac 12 \end{align} As a result: \[ \lim\limits_{x\to (-1)^-} g(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to (-1)^+} g(x) \] Therefore, the limit of $g(x)$ at $x=-1$ exists: \[ \lim\limits_{x \to (-1)} g(x) = \dfrac 12 \:\:{\color{green}\checkmark} \]

  • Statement III is false. Indeed, we have that $\lim\limits_{x \to (-1)} g(x) = \dfrac 12 \neq g(-1).$ $\:\: {\color{red}\times}$

  • Statement IV is true. Since not all statements I-III are true, the function $g(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=-1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and IV only."

example.title: Verifying Continuity at a Point Using the Definition

question.text:
Consider the following function: \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} 36-x^3, & x \lt3 \\ 9, & x= 3 \\ x^2, & x \gt 3 \end{cases} \]

Which of the following statements are true regarding $f(x)?$

  1. $f(x)$ is defined at $x=3$
  2. $\lim\limits_{x\to 3^-} f(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to 3^+} f(x)$
  3. $\lim\limits_{x\to 3} f(x)= f(3)$
  4. $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=3$
question.explanation:
To test for continuity of $f(x)$ at a point $x=c$, we need to check three conditions:

  1. Does $f(c)$ exist?

  2. Does $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)$ exist?

  3. Does $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x) = f(c)?$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Using the expression for the second branch of the function, we obtain that \[ f(3)= 9. \] So, $f(x)$ is defined at $x=3.$ $\:\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Statement II is true. By calculating the one-sided limits, we get the following: \begin{align*} \lim_\limits{ x\to 3^-} f(x) &= \lim_\limits{ x\to 3^-}(36-x^3) \\[5pt] &= 36-(3)^3\\[5pt] &=9 \\[10pt] \lim_\limits{ x\to 3^+} f(x) &= \lim_\limits{ x\to 3^+} (x^2) \\[5pt] &=(3)^2\\[5pt] &= 9 \end{align*} As a result: \[ \lim\limits_{x\to 3^-} f(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to 3^+} f(x) \] Therefore, the limit of $f(x)$ at $x=3$ exists: \[ \lim\limits_{x \to 3} f(x) = 9 \:\:{\color{green}\checkmark} \]

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, we have that $\lim\limits_{x \to 3} f(x) = 9 = f(3).$ $\:\: {\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Statement IV is false. Since all statements I-III are true, according to the continuity test, the function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying the Reason for a Discontinuity

question.text: For what reason does the function $f(x)$ given below have a discontinuity at $x=-2?$ \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} -\dfrac{2}{x+2}, & x \lt -2 \\[5pt] \dfrac{2}{x+2}, & x \gt -2 \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-2.$

  • We have that $f(-2)$ is not defined since $x=-2$ does not belong to the domain of $f(x).$ ${\color{red}\times}$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x = -2$ because $f(-2)$ does not exist.

example.title: Identifying the Reason for a Discontinuity

question.text: For what reason does the function $f(x)$ below have a discontinuity at $x = -\sqrt{3}?$ \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^2+3}{3}, & x \lt -\sqrt{3} \\[5pt] 3, & x = -\sqrt{3} \\[5pt] \dfrac{12}{x^2+3}, & x \gt -\sqrt{3} \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-\sqrt{3}.$

  • $f(-\sqrt{3}) = 3,$ so $f(-\sqrt{3})$ exists. ${\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • We calculate the one-sided limits and find that they coincide: \begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x\to (-\sqrt{3})^-} f(x) &= \lim_\limits{x\to (-\sqrt{3})^-} \left(\dfrac{x^2+3}{3}\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{(-\sqrt{3})^2+3}{3}\\[5pt] & = 2, \\[10pt] \lim_\limits{x\to (-\sqrt{3})^+} f(x) &= \lim_\limits{x\to (-\sqrt{3})^+} \left(\dfrac{12}{x^2+3}\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{12}{(-\sqrt{3})^2+3}\\[5pt] & = 2. \end{align*} Therefore, the overall limit exists and $\lim_\limits{x \to (-\sqrt{3})} f(x) = 2.\, \, {\color{green}\checkmark}$ $\\ \\[1ex]$

  • The limit of the function is not equal to the function value: $\lim_\limits{x \to (-\sqrt{3})} f(x)= 2,$ while $f(-\sqrt{3}) = 3.$ ${\color{red}\times}$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x = -\sqrt{3}$ because $\lim_\limits{x \to (-\sqrt{3})} f(x) \neq f(-\sqrt{3}).$

exampleAnswers.title: Applying the Definition of Continuity to Evaluate a Limit

question.text: If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x = -2$ and $f(-2) = 2,$ then
question.explanation:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-2.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that $\lim\limits_{x\to -2} f(x)$ exists and \[ \lim_{x\to -2^-} f(x) = \lim_{x\to -2} f(x)=f(-2)=2. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to -2^-} \left(x^3+2(f(x))^2\right)} & = (-2)^3 +2(-2)^2 = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0}. \end{align*}

example.title: Applying the Definition of Continuity to Evaluate a Limit

question.text: If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x =2$ and $f(2) = -3,$ what is the value of \[ \displaystyle{\lim_{x \to 2} \left(f^2(x) - 3x\right)^3} \, ? \]
question.explanation:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x = 2.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that $\lim\limits_{x \to 2} f(x)$ exists, and \[ \lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = f(2) = -3. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{x \to 2} \left(f^2(x) - 3x\right)^3} & = \left(f^2(2) - 3 \cdot 2\right)^3\\[3pt] & = \left( (-3)^2 - 3 \cdot 2\right)^3\\[3pt] & = (9 - 6)^3\\[3pt] & = 3^3\\[3pt] & = 27. \end{align*}
